extracted.intended_audience: model aeroplane competitors, club organisers, and hobbyist builders
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance, scoring criteria, data-recording forms, and practical advice for preparing models and competing in organised model aeroplane events (distance, stability, height, steering, gliding, and all-round awards).

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental Data Form I (flight measurements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Column headings A-K: A: Model; B: Weight; C: Area of Supporting Surface; D: Aspect Ratio; E: Average Length of Flight in Feet; F: Maximum Flight; G: Time of Flight, A. average; H: M. maximum; I: Kind and Direction of Wind; J: Camber; K: Angle of Inclination of Main Aerofoil to Line of Flight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form supplied as a standard template to record per-trial flight data; intended to be filled in by the reader and submitted to aeronautical journals when carefully established.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental Data Form I -- motor/propeller continuation
rubrics_metrics.description: Continuation column headings A-L: A: Model; B: Weight of (Rubber) Motor; C: Kind of Rubber, Flat, Square or Round; D: Length in Inches and Number of Strands; E: Number of Turns; F: Condition at End of Flight; G: Number of Propellers (No.) and Diameter (Diam.); H: Number of Blades; I: Disc Area (DiscA.) and Pitch (Pitch); J: Percentage of Slip; K: Thrust; L: Torque in Inche-Ounces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this continuation form to record motor and propeller specifics and performance-related measures for each trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Longest flight (distance measured in straight line)
rubrics_metrics.description: Longest flight measured in a straight line (sometimes both with and against the wind).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All flights to be measured in a straight line from the starting to the landing point; straight-line measurement is essential because curving flights can greatly overstate apparent performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stability (longitudinal and transverse)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stability (both longitudinal and transverse) as a judged quality in competitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stability is an independent test and is one of the principal components used in all-round scoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Longest glide from a given height (no power)
rubrics_metrics.description: Longest glide when launched from a given height without power, but with motor and propeller attached.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often measured by allowing the model to fall from a specified height (example: 20 ft) and recording horizontal distance/angle of glide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Steering (directional control)
rubrics_metrics.description: Steering: the model's ability to follow directed paths or pass near a specified point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "Directional control" can mean launching in a specified direction and passing as near as possible over an indicated point; the author considers directional control particularly difficult and important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greatest height
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure of the greatest altitude attained by the model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Height should be arrived at by observation (not guesswork); helicopters are recommended where a greatest-height prize exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best all-round model (including excellence in building)
rubrics_metrics.description: An aggregate award for a model showing excellence across multiple tests, including construction quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All-round awards aggregate marks from several tests (distance, stability, directional control, gliding/duration) and may reward superiority in building and reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model class by total surface area
rubrics_metrics.description: Models divided into classes by total supporting surface: A: 1 sq. ft. and under; B: 2 sq. ft.; C: 4 sq. ft.; D: 8 sq. ft.; E: over 8 sq. ft.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All surfaces, whether vertical, horizontal, or otherwise, are to be calculated together for classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: All-round efficiency scoring (typical percentage breakdown)
rubrics_metrics.description: Marks or points as percentages for all-round efficiency: Distance 40 per cent.; Stability 35 per cent.; Directional control 15 per cent.; Gliding angle 10 per cent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to award an all-round efficiency prize; alternative allocations (e.g., 10% for duration instead of gliding angle) are noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author's suggested all-round breakdown
rubrics_metrics.description: Author's opinion for all-round efficiency marking: (A) distance and stability 50 per cent.; (B) directional control 30 per cent.; (C) duration of flight 20 per cent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under this scheme, A is launched in any direction; B is as directed by judges; C requires no separate flights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competition trial and measurement rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Competition procedural rules: every competitor allowed three trials in each competition, the best only to count; all flights measured in a straight line from starting to landing point; repairs may be made during the competition at the direction of the judges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competitors should be aware of local variations; judges may permit repairs; failing to be ready in time can lead to disqualification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Launch rules (starting circle and hand launch)
rubrics_metrics.description: Competitors usually requested to start their models from within a given circle (example: six feet diameter) and fly them in any direction they please; models are practically always launched by hand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some organisers prefer to allow contestant to choose direction; where directional control is being judged the judges may specify launch direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kite and Model Aeroplane Association alternative test battery
rubrics_metrics.description: Example competition under K. & M.A.A. rules for best all-round model (machines not under 2 sq. ft. surface): tests (50 marks each): A. Longest flight in a straight line; B. Circular flight to the right; C. Circular flight to the left; D. Stability and landing after a flight; E. Excellence in building of the model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each of these tests is weighted equally (50 marks) in that example; demonstrates alternative test designs used by associations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competitor preparation: fly straight is essential
rubrics_metrics.description: It is absolutely essential that your model should be capable of flying (approximately) straight; distance is measured in a straight line so curving flights reduce credited performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author stresses that many models that fly far but return near the start still score poorly on straight-line measurement; directional control and straight flight are critical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competitor preparation: enter more than one model
rubrics_metrics.description: Always enter more than one model; there nearly always is an entrance fee but extras are worthwhile to increase chances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple entries hedge against failures or poor suitability of one design on the day.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competitor preparation: arrive early and test on site
rubrics_metrics.description: Always make it a point of arriving early on the ground so that you can make some trial flights beforehand; every ground has local peculiarities of air currents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Familiarity with the competition ground and local wind patterns can materially affect performance and selection of model to fly that day.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competitor preparation: be ready and have an assistant
rubrics_metrics.description: Always be ready in time, or you may be disqualified; if flying a twin-screw model use a special winder and take a competent friend as assistant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preparation of equipment for quick servicing and synchronized winding (for twin screws) is recommended to avoid delays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliability requirement for all-round efficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: For all-round efficiency nothing but a good all-round model, which can be absolutely relied on to make a dozen (approximately) equivalent flights, is any good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistency across multiple flights is a key criterion for all-round awards; one-off exceptional flights are less valuable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum-performance advice for open distance competitions
rubrics_metrics.description: In an open distance competition, unless you have a model which you can rely on to make a minimum flight of 200 yards, do not enter unless you know none of the top flyers will be present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is tactical advice to avoid wasting entries/fees against stronger competitors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competitor checklist: spare parts and tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not neglect the smallest detail likely to lead to success; be prepared with spare parts, extra rubber, one or two handy tools, wire, thread, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preparedness can prevent avoidable retirements; the author cites Faraday's habit of preparing for lectures as an analogy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight-rating strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: If the rating of the model is by weight (1 oz., 2 oz., 4 oz., etc.) and not area, use a model weighing from 10 oz. to a pound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select model weight strategically to maximise competitiveness within a weight-class competition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Landing robustness requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Model should be able to 'land' without damage and, as far as possible, on an even keel; include some form of 'skid' or 'shock-absorber' rather than omitting for weight saving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Especially important for biplanes; inability to land safely may restrict number of flights to one and ruin competition prospects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjustable angle to reconcile gliding and flying angles
rubrics_metrics.description: Since the best 'gliding' angle and 'flying' angle are not the same (example: gliding ~7°, flying ~1°-3°), an adjustable angle might in some cases be advantageous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Providing means to change incidence/angle between powered and gliding configurations can improve performance across different tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Testing motors consistently
rubrics_metrics.description: To test different motors or different powers of the same kind of motor, test them on the same machine and do not use different motors or different powers on different machines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Control variables: keep airframe constant when comparing motor performance for valid comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation static thrust to total weight
rubrics_metrics.description: Relation between static thrust of propeller and total weight of model: the thrust should be approximately equal to 1/4 of the weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design guideline for selecting propeller and motor to enable take-off/vertical capability for self-raising models or helicopters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method to determine experimentally the static thrust of a propeller
rubrics_metrics.description: Mount propeller on shaft of electric motor (1000–1500 rpm) placed on scales or spring balance with axis vertical; rotate propeller to drive air upwards; measure reaction as difference in scale reading (or balance with weights) at the indicated speed to obtain thrust in ounces or pounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record voltage and amperage with and without propeller to compute power absorbed by propeller; adjust for motor losses (e.g., deduct ~10%) to estimate propeller-driven watts and convert to horsepower (746 W = 1 h.p.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use formula for comparing models (performance index)
rubrics_metrics.description: To compare one model with another the formula Weight × velocity (in ft. per sec.) / horse-power is sometimes useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This composite metric helps evaluate efficiency by combining weight, speed and power; complementary to direct measurements of thrust and lift.

rubrics_metrics.name: Efficiency depends on weight per horsepower
rubrics_metrics.description: The efficiency of a model depends on the weight carried per h.p.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lower weight per available power generally yields higher achievable performance for a given design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Efficiency of design depends on supporting surface at given speed
rubrics_metrics.description: The efficiency of some particular design depends on the amount of supporting surface necessary at a given speed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designs that require less supporting surface for the same speed are more efficient in terms of drag and power requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Horsepower rating formula for model petrol motors
rubrics_metrics.description: Formula for rating horse-power of model petrol motors: H.P. = ((Bore)^2 × stroke × no. of cylinders × R.P.M.) / 12,000.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the computed right-hand side gives less h.p. than stated for a motor, then the motor's rated h.p. is likely over-estimated.
